title: Mitigation of Karenia brevis Cells and Brevetoxins Using Curcumin, a Natural Supplement
scale: 1.5 L beakers and 10 L aquaria; 13 experiments
result: 5 mg/L: -89% cells at 24 h and -60% toxin; 0.1-2 mg/L no different from each other; 30-40 mg/L >90% reduction by 4 h.
env_effects: pH, salinity, temperature and DO stable except the ethanol experiment (DO fell to 1.55 mg/L by 48 h, bacterial bloom); nutrients unchanged; water turned yellow to dark orange.

title: Lessons learned from mesocosm experiments with curcumin: Pilot studies of a harmful algal bloom mitigation technique
organism: Karenia brevis; hard clams, sea urchins, blue crabs
scale: 1,400 L fiberglass mesocosms at the Mote RTMTDI facility, Sarasota FL (6 tanks in March 2022, 12 in January 2024; 3 curcumin-treated tanks each year), cultured K. brevis
duration: up to 72 h (both runs cut short by bacterial blooms, K. brevis crashes and hypoxia at 48-72 h)
result: 2022: cells -86% at 24 h and -99% at 48 h, total brevetoxins -65% and -74%; 2024: cells only -32% at 24 h and -47% at 48 h, toxins -46% and -7%; no measured effects on clams, urchins or crabs within 72 h.
env_effects: No measured impacts on hard clams, sea urchins or blue crabs within 72 h (2024 run; 4 clams, 4 urchins, 3 crabs per tank). Bacterial blooms and hypoxia (<2 mg/L) appeared in all groups including controls, attributed to a facility-wide problem.
key_details: Two pilot runs in 1,400 L mesocosms dosed with 5 mg/L curcumin, three treated tanks per run; only 2024 had curcumin-only and seawater controls. Changes were measured relative to each tank's time-0 value and compared with Karenia controls (Kruskal-Wallis). In 2022 cells fell 86.34% at 24 h (control +18.52%) and 99.22% at 48 h (control +70.79%); in 2024 the reduction was significant only at 6 h (-27.35%) and reached just 47% at 48 h, with toxin reduction fluctuating (-5.39% to -45.66%) and ending at -7.56%. Both runs were cut short by bacterial blooms, Karenia control crashes to 0 cells/L and hypoxia; affected tanks were discarded, and one 2024 treated tank crashed, leaving n = 2 at 48 h. The authors frame the study as lessons learned about mesocosm methods; the year-to-year inconsistency and small n make the efficacy estimate weak.
fulltext_discrepancy: Abstract-based record said percentages were not given and implied consistent drops; the full text shows a 99% cell cut in 2022 but only 47% (and 7% toxin) in 2024, with runs compromised by bacterial blooms and hypoxia.

title: Inhibition of five natural products from Chinese herbs on the growth of Chattonella marina
scale: 100 mL flasks with 50 mL culture; initial 4.4 x 10^6 cells/L; n=3
dose: each of 5 compounds at 10 mg/L (curcumin dissolved in ethanol; ethanol solvent control); gramine further at 0.32-3 mg/L
result: At 10 mg/L curcumin was the second-strongest inhibitor of C. marina, with an inhibitory rate similar to gramine at 72 h, but it was dropped from further study because it turned the medium yellow. Gramine LC50 was 1.12, 0.77, 0.58 and 0.51 mg/L at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h.
env_effects: Curcumin turned the culture medium yellow, which the authors flag as a potential adverse impact on the aquatic environment.
key_details: Batch cultures of C. marina in f/2 at 20 °C, 12:12 h light; five Chinese-herb compounds (evodiamine, 4-methoxysalicylaldehyde, gramine, esculin hydrate, curcumin) each added at 10 mg/L, with ethanol/acetone solvent controls, n=3, cell counts by hemocytometer at 24/48/72 h. Gramine had the highest inhibitory rate, curcumin a similar one; evodiamine gave 40% at 72 h and the other two little inhibition. Only gramine was studied further (Fv/Fm, Chl a, SOD/CAT, MDA); 3 mg/L gramine gave 80% inhibition within 150 min. The curcumin inhibition percentage is shown only in Fig. 1 and is not stated numerically in the text.
fulltext_discrepancy: The 80% at 10 mg/L (72 h) figure for curcumin comes from a secondary citation; the paper's text gives no number for curcumin (Fig. 1 only), just 'similar inhibitory rate as gramine'. The 96 h LC50 0.51 mg/L is gramine's, not curcumin's; curcumin had no dose-response work.

title: Targeting Florida red tide: Curcumin inhibits Karenia brevis thioredoxin reductase
organism: Recombinant Karenia brevis thioredoxin reductase (KbTrxR, expressed in E. coli)
result: Curcumin inhibited KbTrxR in a time-dependent way: IC50 fell from 111.0 uM to 3.0 uM after 60 min pre-incubation (~20x more potent than PbTx-2); inhibition also seen with H2O2 as substrate; covalent adduct at Cys53.
env_effects: n/a (mechanism).
key_details: Purely in vitro enzyme study on synthetic recombinant KbTrxR; no live K. brevis cells were treated. DTNB-reduction and H2O2-reduction assays run in triplicate; IC50 by nonlinear regression. LC-MS/MS located the curcumin adduct at N-terminal Cys53. Authors cite prior work that 0.1-5 mg/L curcumin reduces K. brevis 2-89% in 24 h, and note enzyme IC50 is not comparable with whole-cell toxicity.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's 3.0 uM IC50 is only after 60 min pre-incubation; without it the IC50 was 111.0 uM. Enzyme was recombinant, not from cells.

title: Inhibition of Diarrheal Shellfish Toxins Accumulation in the Mussel Perna viridis by Curcumin and Underlying Mechanisms
organism: mussel Perna viridis fed Prorocentrum lima
scale: lab; mussels in 6 L seawater; digestive glands of 6 mussels pooled per sample, n = 3 samples per group
dose: Prorocentrum lima 2 x 10^6 cells/L; curcumin 0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 umol/L (step I); 20 umol/L (step II)
result: Curcumin at 10 and 20 umol/L significantly lowered DST (okadaic acid-eq) in the digestive gland vs no curcumin (p<0.05), with more DST found in the water instead; gill DST unchanged. Curcumin reduced P. lima-induced digestive-gland damage.
env_effects: Curcumin alone (20 uM) caused no visible digestive-gland damage in mussels. Curcumin was dissolved in NaOH; solvent given to controls. Does not reduce the algae; it is a shellfish-detox approach.
key_details: Two-step lab design with Perna viridis (8-10 cm) fed Tetraselmis plus toxic P. lima (CCMP 2579). Step I: curcumin dose series, DST by ELISA at 48 h. Step II: 4 groups (control, curcumin, P. lima, P. lima + curcumin at 20 uM), sampled at 12 and 48 h for DST, qPCR (AhR, HR96, CYP3A4) and histology. Pooled samples give only n = 3 per group; % reductions are shown only in figures. Mechanism proposed: curcumin blocks toxin-induced transcription of AhR/HR96/CYP3A4.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record dose/duration 'not in abstract' -> 1-50 uM curcumin, 48 h. Effective doses were 10-20 uM (~3.7-7.4 mg/L). Toxin appears to be moved to the water, not destroyed.

title: The Chemistry of Curcumin: From Extraction to Therapeutic Agent
result: λmax 410-430 nm; pKa1 7.5-8.5 (anion absorbs at 467 nm); logP ~3; 90% of µM solutions degrade in 30 min; much faster fading in sunlight.
env_effects: Breakdown products vanillin, ferulic acid and small phenols.

title: Stability of curcumin in buffer solutions and characterization of its degradation products
venue: Journal of Pharmaceutical and Biomedical Analysis
result: About 90% decomposed within 30 min at pH 7.2; faster at neutral-basic pH; serum proteins slow it (~50% left at 8 h).
env_effects: Breakdown products vanillin, ferulic acid.

title: Physical and Chemical Stability of Curcumin in Aqueous Solutions and Emulsions: Impact of pH, Temperature, and Molecular Environment
venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
scale: 40 µM curcumin in 10 mM phosphate buffer (pH 2.0-8.0) in a cuvette; MCT oil-in-water emulsions (30 wt% oil, Tween 80, 0.285 mg/mL curcumin, pH 3.0-8.0)
duration: buffer solutions: minutes to 60 min at 37 °C; emulsions: 31 days at 37 °C (plus other temperatures)
result: In buffer at pH ≥7.0 curcumin degraded rapidly in the first 7 min (initial rates 92, 135 and 125 cm-1/min at pH 7.0, 7.4, 8.0), while at pH <7 it crystallized (10-50 µm crystals). In MCT emulsions 85-95% remained after 31 days at acidic pH but only 53-62% at pH ≥7.0.
env_effects: Not reported.
key_details: Spectrophotometric (433 nm) degradation and turbidity (600 nm) assays of 40 µM curcumin (added from a DMSO stock) in phosphate buffers at 37 °C, with and without stirring; emulsion storage over 31 days at several pH values and temperatures. Stirring promoted crystallization and aggregation of crystals in acidic solutions; alkaline solutions stayed clear but faded fast. Oil solubility of pure curcumin in MCT was 2.90 mg/g; in bulk MCT at 55 °C for 31 days there was no significant loss, so degradation happens at the oil-water interface. Water solubility of curcumin is cited as 11 ng/mL. Caveat for HAB use: seawater pH (~8) is the regime where free curcumin degrades within minutes.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record is broadly correct. Retention after 31 days at 37 °C was 53-62% for pH 7.0-8.0 (the per-pH 62/60/53 split is from Fig. 3B, not stated in text). Crystals formed at pH 3, 5 and 7, not only below pH 7.

title: Influence of vehicle properties and excipients on hydrolytic and photochemical stability of curcumin in preparations containing Pluronics: Studies of curcumin and curcuminoids XLVIII
result: Hydrolysis faster at pH 8.0-8.8 and in carbonate buffer; ethanol lowered stability; photochemical half-life 'in the minutes range'.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Studies of curcumin and curcuminoids. XXVII. Cyclodextrin complexation: solubility, chemical and photochemical stability
scale: aqueous buffer solutions with six cyclodextrins (HPαCD, HPβCD, HPγCD, RMβCD, SBβCD, HTAβCD), mostly 5% w/v; xenon-lamp photolysis; n=3
dose: cyclodextrin 1-5%; hydrolysis tested at pH 8.0, complexation at pH 5
duration: minutes (photolysis, hydrolysis of free curcumin) to days (complexed curcumin)
result: Complexation raised curcumin's water solubility about 10^4-fold at pH 5 and dramatically improved hydrolytic stability at alkaline pH (free curcumin half-life a few minutes above pH 7; 5% HPβCD complex half-life 19.8 days at pH 5). Photostability fell: photolysis half-lives were 20.4-46.2 min in 5% cyclodextrins versus 70.7 min in ethanol-buffer and 133.3 min in methanol.
env_effects: Not reported.
key_details: Phase-solubility and kinetic study of curcumin with six neutral or charged cyclodextrins at room temperature. RMβCD and HPγCD gave the highest affinity, cationic HTAβCD the lowest; neutral cyclodextrins protected against hydrolysis better than charged ones. The most stable pH 8 sample (5% HPβCD) degraded at 0.035 per day at pH 5 (half-life 19.8 d, n=3). Photodegradation followed first-order kinetics and was faster in every cyclodextrin than in organic solvent systems. No algae or organisms tested.

title: On the photobehaviour of curcumin in biocompatible hosts: The role of H-abstraction in the photodegradation and photosensitization
venue: Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology B: Biology
scale: curcumin in Pluronic micelles, microemulsions and zein nanoparticles; steady-state photolysis (anaerobic, visible light), 1O2 luminescence, laser flash photolysis; dioxane as reference solvent
result: No singlet oxygen was detected from curcumin in any host (only in dioxane); the triplet of the diketo form abstracts hydrogen from the host, giving ketyl radicals that react with O2 to form peroxyl radicals. The authors argue curcumin is a poor photosensitizer and its phototoxicity is probably radical-mediated, not 1O2-mediated.
env_effects: Not reported.
key_details: Spectroscopic study of curcumin encapsulated in three biocompatible hosts, which shifted its keto-enol equilibrium towards the diketo form. Photolysis was run anaerobically under visible light and 1O2 phosphorescence was measured in each host and in dioxane. A clear 1O2 signal appeared in dioxane but none in any host, partly because the triplet lifetime in the hosts is too short for oxygen quenching to compete. The authors note curcumin absorbs only blue light, has ISC/1O2 quantum yields of ca. 0.1 at most in organic solvents, reacts readily with 1O2 and is poorly water-soluble. No organisms tested.

title: Back to the roots: photodynamic inactivation of bacteria based on water-soluble curcumin bound to polyvinylpyrrolidone as a photosensitizer
result: 5 µM (≈1.8 mg/L) gave >6 log10 kill of S. aureus; 50 µM for 15-25 min eradicated it; longer pre-incubation was less phototoxic.
env_effects: E. coli needed CaCl2 to open the cell wall.

title: Curcumin Affects Development of Zebrafish Embryo
duration: 24 h LD50; embryos followed daily to hatching, larvae exposed from 3 d old
result: 24 h LD50 7.5 uM for embryos and 5 uM for larvae; 15 uM killed all embryos within 2 d and 10 uM killed all larvae; embryos at >=5 uM developed bent/hooked tails, spinal curvature, pericardial edema, retarded yolk resorption.
env_effects: Lethal below the 5 mg/L algal dose.
key_details: Zebrafish embryos (from 30 min post-fertilization) and 3-day-old larvae exposed in 6-well plates, 10 embryos per well; 30 animals x 4 replicates per concentration. Survival judged by heartbeat. Resveratrol, quercetin and rutin up to 100 uM had no effect. Curcumin decomposed in water over 2-3 d, which the authors used to explain survival differences. No DMSO-only solvent control is described.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record essentially correct; adds that teratogenic effects began at 5 uM and no solvent control is reported.

title: Environmental safety and mode of action of a novel curcumin-based photolarvicide
organism: Aedes aegypti larvae (target); Daphnia magna, Danio rerio (zebrafish) and Pseudokirchneriella subcapitata feeding (non-target)
dose: three formulations: curcumin in 1% DMSO/99% ethanol (1.5 mg/mL stock), or 1% curcumin in 99% sucrose or 99% D-mannitol (w/w); non-target tests up to 100 mg/L; larvae 0.45-5.4 mg/L
duration: Daphnia 24-48 h (acute), 6 h (sub-lethal); zebrafish 48 h; larvae up to 8 h natural sunlight
result: The ethanol+DMSO formulation gave a zebrafish LC50 of 5.9 mg/L (2.55-13.6) and its solvents killed >10% of Daphnia in the solvent control; the sucrose and D-mannitol formulations were practically non-toxic to Daphnia and zebrafish even at 100 mg/L. Sugar formulations killed 100% of Aedes larvae at 0.45, 1.8 and 5.4 mg/L after 8 h of sunlight.
env_effects: Daphnia at 50 mg/L showed a 59% rise in ROS; at 50 mg/L of the D-mannitol formulation algal growth in the Daphnia feeding test was 117% of control; curcumin adhered to Daphnia bodies and guts at 100 mg/L. Solvent carrier was more toxic than curcumin.
key_details: Tested a curcumin photolarvicide in three carriers on non-target D. magna (OECD 202, in dark and 16:8 light, n=35 for sub-lethal assays) and zebrafish (10 fish per replicate, n=20), plus target Aedes aegypti larvae in natural sunlight. The ethanol+DMSO formulation was judged unfeasible for field use and not tested on larvae. Sugar-carrier formulations showed no acute toxicity to Daphnia at 100 mg/L and were non-toxic to fish, while killing all larvae at 0.45 mg/L and above within 8 h of sunlight; larvae were lethargic after 1 h. Larval CAT and GSH changes were measured for the D-mannitol formulation. No harmful algae were tested; relevant to curcumin as an outdoor photosensitizer's non-target safety.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the target organism (Aedes aegypti larvae) and the 100 mg/L no-effect level of the sugar formulations; 'Duration: Not reported' is wrong (24-48 h acute tests, 8 h sunlight larval tests).

title: Environmentally Safe Photodynamic Control of Aedes aegypti Using Sunlight-Activated Synthetic Curcumin: Photodegradation, Aquatic Ecotoxicity, and Field Trial
result: LT50 3 d in sunlight and no toxicity in the dark; cited LC50-3h 2.2-20 mg/L and LC50-24h 0.04 mg/L in sun.
env_effects: Animal toxicity is light-gated; photoproduct toxicity only predicted (ECOSAR), not measured.

title: Biocompatibility Study of Curcumin-Loaded Pluronic F127 Nanoformulation (NanoCUR) against the Embryonic Development of Zebrafish (Danio rerio)
dose: native curcumin 1-100 uM vs NanoCUR (Pluronic F127) 1-100 uM; Pluronic F127 alone to 2% w/v
result: Native curcumin LC50 fell from 8.077 uM at 24 hpf to 6.302 uM at 96 hpf; NanoCUR LC50 was >100 uM through 72 hpf and 28.4 uM at 96 hpf; 10 uM native curcumin left 41% survival at 24 hpf and 20% at 72 hpf; >30 uM killed 100% by 24 hpf.
env_effects: Native curcumin toxic to zebrafish embryos at ~6 uM (~2.3 mg/L); nano-encapsulation cut toxicity ~4.5x at 96 h; carrier alone non-toxic.
key_details: Zebrafish embryo toxicity test comparing native curcumin, curcumin-loaded Pluronic F127 micelles and the carrier alone; endpoints survival, hatching, heart rate, malformations (yolk-sac edema, scoliosis) and ROS. At least three independent experiments. 1 uM native curcumin gave 100% survival. Drug-delivery context, not HAB treatment.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record had no numbers; full text gives native curcumin 96 h LC50 6.302 uM vs 28.4 uM for NanoCUR.

title: The effectiveness of five natural products against three species of harmful algae
organism: Chattonella marina, Alexandrium tamarense, Karenia mikimotoi
scale: 100 mL beakers with 50 mL culture; f/2, 20 °C, 12:12 h light; initial ~5-6, 3-4 and 7-8 x 10^6 cells/L (C. marina, A. tamarense, K. mikimotoi)
dose: screen: ε-polylysine, berberine, stachydrine, betaine, chitosan each at 50 mg/L; LC50 series; berberine 10-30 mg/L short-term; 4 and 8 mg/L for TEM
result: At 50 mg/L only berberine inhibited K. mikimotoi (IR nearly 100% in 24 h; LC50-120h 3.1 mg/L), ε-polylysine was best on C. marina (70.9% at 120 h; LC50-120h 29.2 mg/L), and betaine and stachydrine were best on A. tamarense (LC50-120h 17.8 and 20.0 mg/L). Chitosan's apparent effect matched its acetic-acid control.
env_effects: Not reported.
key_details: Screen of five natural products (no curcumin) against three marine HAB species with water and acetic-acid controls; cell counts at 24-120 h; means ± SD with t-tests (replicate number not stated in text). Selectivity was strong: berberine LC50-120h was 3.1 mg/L on K. mikimotoi but 71.9 mg/L on C. marina and 58.5 mg/L on A. tamarense. Berberine at 30 mg/L inhibited K. mikimotoi within 120 min; at 10 mg/L IR was ≤40% and at 20 mg/L nearly 60% in 120 min. TEM showed organelle dissolution at 4 mg/L and membrane rupture at 8 mg/L within 12 h. No non-target toxicity tests were done, though the authors call berberine environmentally safe.
fulltext_discrepancy: Dose was reported (50 mg/L screen), not missing. The paper contains no curcumin. Nearly 100% K. mikimotoi inhibition by berberine at 50 mg/L in 24 h was omitted.

title: Comparing effects of berberine on the growth and photosynthetic activities of Microcystis aeruginosa and Chlorella pyrenoidosa
scale: lab cultures in BG11, triplicates, 12:12 light-dark vs constant dark
dose: 4 mg/L berberine (growth tests); 24 h-EC50 on M. aeruginosa 0.47 mg/L
result: Under light-dark, 4 mg/L berberine drove M. aeruginosa cell density to zero by day 6, with Fv/Fm and ETR near zero after 1 day; it had no effect in constant darkness and no effect on Chlorella pyrenoidosa in either condition.
env_effects: Not reported.
key_details: Lab monocultures of Microcystis aeruginosa and Chlorella pyrenoidosa were exposed to 4 mg/L berberine (an allelochemical) in triplicate for 9 days under 12:12 light-dark or constant dark, with untreated controls. In light, M. aeruginosa density fell to zero by day 6 and Fv/Fm dropped to 0.04 within 10 h; in darkness there was no algicidal effect. The 24 h-EC50 for M. aeruginosa was 0.47 mg/L, which cut true photosynthesis (131.20 to 107.82 umol O2/mg Chl a/h) but not dark respiration. C. pyrenoidosa growth and photosynthesis were unaffected. Single strains in culture medium; no natural community, toxin or non-target animal data.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record listed dose and duration as 'Not reported'; the paper used 4 mg/L for 9 days (EC50 0.47 mg/L) and reached complete Microcystis elimination by day 6.

title: Effect of environmental factors on allelopathic inhibition of Microcystis aeruginosa by berberine
result: Strongest when light and temperature favoured growth; 'hardly' algicidal in darkness.
env_effects: Raised extracellular microcystin by lysing cells.

title: Physiological and Molecular Response of Prorocentrum minimum to Tannic Acid: An Experimental Study to Evaluate the Feasibility of Using Tannic Acid in Controling the Red Tide in a Eutrophic Coastal Water
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
result: Growth normal below 2.5 mg/L and slowed above it; 10 mg/L halted photosynthesis; Hsp70/Hsp90 up 10-27× at 48 h.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Effects of Dihydroartemisinin and Artemether on the Growth, Chlorophyll Fluorescence, and Extracellular Alkaline Phosphatase Activity of the Cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa
dose: dihydroartemisinin 6, 12, 24 mg/L; artemether results reported at 6 mg/L
result: After 120 h, growth inhibition peaked at 16.67%, 35.94% and 42.17% for 6, 12 and 24 mg/L dihydroartemisinin and 55.72% for 6 mg/L artemether; with artemether Fv/Fm, PhiPSII, ETR and rETRmax fell to 0.
env_effects: Not reported.
key_details: Axenic lab culture of Microcystis aeruginosa in 300 mL BG11, treated vs untreated controls, three replicates. Measured cell density (0-120 h), chlorophyll a, protein, MDA, alkaline phosphatase and chlorophyll fluorescence. Partial growth inhibition only (max ~56%). Compounds are artemisinin derivatives, not curcumin.
fulltext_discrepancy: This paper is about dihydroartemisinin and artemether, not curcumin; it probably belongs in a different method bucket. Effect_pct can be set to 55.72 (artemether) or 42.17 (dihydroartemisinin).

title: Physiological and molecular mechanisms of the inhibitory effects of artemisinin on Microcystis aeruginosa and Chlorella pyrenoidosa
result: Artemisinin blocks the QB site and ferredoxin-NADP⁺ reductase, causing ROS build-up; Chlorella resists.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Growth, physiological responses and microcystin-production/-release dynamics of Microcystis aeruginosa exposed to various luteolin doses
scale: 250 mL flasks with 100 mL BG11, initial 4 x 10^5 cells/mL, 25 °C, 12:12 h; triplicate
dose: luteolin (DMSO stock) 0.5-32 mg/L range-finding; then 3.25, 6.5 and 13 mg/L (0.5x, 1x, 2x IC50)
result: IC50 was stable at 6.342-6.810 mg/L from day 8 to 14 (about 6.5 mg/L). Growth inhibition in the mid-late stage held at 38-60%, 52-62% and 70-78% for 3.25, 6.5 and 13 mg/L, and extracellular microcystin fell 5.26-78.35% below control, more at higher doses.
env_effects: Extracellular microcystin decreased at all doses versus control (26.13-61.93% day 4, 5.26-74.21% day 8, 42.99-78.35% day 14); MC-release percentage stayed below 10% early on.
key_details: Toxigenic M. aeruginosa FACHB-915 was exposed to luteolin in BG11 for 14 d with triplicate exposure and control flasks; IC50 was estimated by probit regression on days 8 and 14. At each dose inhibition rose until about day 4-6 then plateaued or fell slightly as cells upregulated CAT and GSH (late-stage stimulation 2.58x and 2.36x). Chlorophyll a was stimulated early (1.21-2.25x on day 4) then inhibited. The IC50 is higher than the 1.85 mg/L reported for a non-toxigenic strain (FACHB-469). Single strain, lab only, DMSO carrier.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies inhibition fell late; the text says it plateaued or dropped only slightly, holding 38-78% by dose. Record says 'Not reported' for microcystin effects, but extracellular MC fell 5-78% versus control.

title: Long-term suppression of Microcystis aeruginosa by tannic acid: Risks of microcystin pollution and proteomic mechanisms
result: High doses inhibit; one intermediate dose raised extracellular MC-LR to 1.91× control on day 15.
env_effects: Toxin release rose at an intermediate dose.

title: Effects of low concentration of gallic acid on the growth and microcystin production of Microcystis aeruginosa
scale: 160 mL BG11 cultures, initial 7 x 10^5 cells/mL, 25 °C, 10:14 h light, shaken 120 rpm; triplicate
duration: about 32 d, sampled every 4 d (transcriptomics at day 32)
result: Gallic acid inhibited growth at ≥1 µg/L (maximum inhibition 73.79% at 10,000 µg/L) but stimulated it at ≤0.1 µg/L (maximum promotion 45.28% at 0.1 µg/L; growth rate 1.09x and maximum density 1.16x control). At 0.1 µg/L microcystin synthesis rose 1.85x and total MCs reached 1.23 mg/L (+54.73%).
env_effects: At 0.1 µg/L, total microcystins +54.73% (1.23 mg/L), intracellular MC per cell 1.77 times higher than control, and the ecological risk quotient was 0.3, about 30x control (moderate risk). At 10,000 µg/L intracellular MC per cell was lower than control.
key_details: Triplicate BG11 cultures of toxigenic M. aeruginosa exposed to eight gallic acid levels spanning 7 orders of magnitude, with cell density, Chl a, ATP, ROS, SYTOX viability, intra- and extracellular MCs and transcriptomics (0.1 and 10,000 µg/L at day 32). The response was hormetic: inhibition at ≥1 µg/L, stimulation at ≤0.1 µg/L, with the inhibitory effect no longer significant above 10 µg/L per the authors' model and peak promotion at 0.18 µg/L. On day 9 the 0.1 µg/L group was 15.5% denser than control; Chl a per cell peaked at +152.85% (day 17). MC-synthesis genes were upregulated at low dose. Caveat: a single strain in lab culture; the authors warn that dilution and degradation of an applied allelochemical can leave stimulating residues.
fulltext_discrepancy: The 1.09x is the growth-rate ratio; the text's headline promotion is 45.28% at 0.1 µg/L (max density 1.16x), so effect_pct -9 understates the stimulation. Duration (~32 d) was reported. High doses did inhibit (73.79% at 10 mg/L).
